HOW: add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The sibling-subdomain check compares everything after the first label, so it also matches unrelated sites under shared suffixes like `co.uk` or `github.io`. WHY: the full URL path is shown for sites that are not the instance's own domain. HOW: compare against the registrable domain, or restrict the match to the `www.` case.

suggestions.label: testing
suggestions.suggestionContent: The `www.example.com` versus `forum.example.com` sibling branch of `website_name` has no spec. This is a coverage gap rather than a defect: it is not a test that passes while the behaviour it names is broken. Consider adding a spec for that branch.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: runSplitQuery interpolates targets, including ad hoc filters, via applyTemplateVariables, but each split sub-request goes through datasource.runQuery and DataSourceWithBackend.query, which calls applyTemplateVariables again with the same request.filters. WHY: ad hoc filters can be injected twice into the expr, and variable values that contain `$` can be re-interpolated, which produces wrong queries. HOW: pass an empty filters argument in the first pass, or skip interpolation in the second pass, so each target is interpolated and filtered exactly once.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: enableSqlExpressions negates the feature flag and then returns false on both paths, so it always returns false. WHY: the flag is never honored and the dead branch hides the real intent, so SQL expressions stay disabled even if the flag is turned on, and the logic misleads maintainers. HOW: either return a constant false with a clear comment for a hard disable, or return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` if the flag should control it.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path. The flag check is inverted into `enabled` and then discarded, so SQL expressions are rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is on. Return the flag's value directly.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path, so the feature flag is ignored and every SQL expression query is rejected, even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Return the flag's actual value, e.g. `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path, including when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. ReadQuery therefore rejects every SQL expression with "sqlExpressions is not implemented" and the feature flag has no effect. It should return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: SQLCommand.Execute used to run the query through duck.DB. It now calls the stub sql.DB, whose QueryFramesInto always returns "not implemented". Any SQL expression that reaches Execute fails, and TablesList in parser.go fails the same way. The consumers were not updated for the loss of the working implementation.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `enableSqlExpressions` reads as a check that the feature is enabled. It stores the negated flag in a variable called `enabled` and always returns false, even when FlagSqlExpressions is on. Rename it to match what it does, or make it return the flag's actual value.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: A denial is cached for shortCacheTTL and the early return at the top of Check skips the permission re-query, so a denied (user, action, name, folder) stays denied until the entry expires. WHY: if a user is granted access, or the resource is created and permissions are assigned right after an earlier check, Check keeps returning Allowed:false for the whole TTL. This is the stale-permission case the PR is meant to fix. HOW: keep the TTL very short or drop it, or invalidate denial entries when permissions change, or on a denial hit re-query at most once per short interval.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: userPermDenialCacheKey joins action, name and parent with '_' and does not escape them, so different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key. For example, name 'a' with parent 'b_c' and name 'a_b' with parent 'c' both give 'a_b_c'. WHY: a denial cached for one resource can wrongly deny access to a different resource. HOW: use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or length-prefix or encode each component.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment says access is allowed to prove the permCache is not consulted, but the map value is `false`, which denies. If the denial cache were ignored, the test would still return denied, so it proves nothing. Set the value to `true` so the test matches the comment.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The denial cache key joins name and parent with '_' without escaping, so different (name, parent) pairs can map to the same key (e.g. name 'a_b'+parent 'c' vs name 'a'+parent 'b_c'). A cached denial for one resource then wrongly denies another that is allowed, until the TTL expires. Use a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs or length-prefix the components.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The deny-entry test seeds permCache with dash1 set to false, although its comment says it grants access to prove the permission cache is not checked. Without the denial-cache short-circuit the request would still be denied, so the test passes with the feature removed. Seed permCache with true so that only the denial entry can produce the deny.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Debug logging at Error level dumps the full ID list and condition for every batch, in all three cleanup paths. WHY: With large batch sizes (up to tens of thousands of IDs) this writes huge log lines and falsely signals errors on every cleanup cycle. HOW: Remove these log calls, or reduce them to a Debug-level count only.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The cleanup ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. WHY: This runs every cleanup job, including the annotation cleanup, 10x more often, adding DB load and lock contention that the PR is trying to reduce. HOW: Restore the 10 minute interval.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: The cleanup loop logs every fetched annotation ID and the raw SQL condition at Error level on every batch, even on success. This dumps internal record identifiers and query text into the logs, with up to batch-size IDs per line. Remove these debug logs, or log only counts at debug level. The same pattern repeats in the count-based and tag cleanup paths.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Routine batch progress is logged with r.log.Error, and it includes the full ID slices. This floods error logs on every cleanup run and reports a non-error as an error. The logged `err` is always nil at that point. Remove these debug logs or lower them to Debug without the ID lists. The same pattern appears in the count and tag cleanup paths.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The cleanup ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This looks like a leftover debugging change that runs all cleanup jobs 10x more often than intended. Restore the 10 minute interval.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: deleteByIDs binds one placeholder per ID on every database except SQLite with a batch size above 999. Postgres and MySQL cap bind parameters at 65535, so a configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above that makes every cleanup batch fail. The old single-statement query had no such limit. Split the ID slice into chunks under the limit before building the IN clause.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The log lines 'Annotations to clean by time' and 'cleaned annotations by time' describe normal progress but are emitted with r.log.Error, so every cleanup batch looks like a failure in the logs. The first also logs err, which is always nil there. The same pattern appears in the count-based and tag cleanup paths. Use Debug (or remove them) and drop the nil err field.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: readInteger passes the result of readLength to read(length) without checking for -1, which readLength returns for an indefinite-length encoding. WHY: a malformed signature makes read() throw NegativeArraySizeException, an unchecked exception, where callers expect an IOException. HOW: throw IOException when length < 0 in readInteger, and in read(int) as well.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: getBouncyCastleProvider() is named and documented in the CryptoProvider contract as returning the BouncyCastle provider. Here it returns whatever JDK provider backs the default KeyStore type (e.g. SUN), so callers that read the name will assume BC features. Add a comment or Javadoc stating that this provider deliberately returns a non-BouncyCastle JDK provider.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The test uses one default (P-256) EC key for ES256, ES384 and ES512, and only round-trips through the same converter. For ES384 and ES512 the r and s values are never full-size (48 or 66 bytes), so the truncation, padding and sign-byte paths are never exercised. A symmetric bug would also go unnoticed. Generate a key on the matching curve for each algorithm (secp256r1, secp384r1, secp521r1) and assert the concatenated length equals signLength. Also verify the re-encoded DER signature with Signature.verify.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: These two ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are never used. The return statement builds new encoders for the same values. Remove the dead computation.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: canManage() accepts the VIEW scope as grounds for managing groups. WHY: an admin who only holds view permission on all groups passes canManage() and can create top-level groups and perform other global manage operations. HOW: check only AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() passes groupResource.getId() (the resource UUID) to hasPermission() and adds that UUID to the result. WHY: hasPermission() looks resources up by name, and group resources are named by group id, so the lookup misses. It then falls back to the all-groups type resource, and the returned set holds resource UUIDs instead of group ids, so the users search filtered by UserModel.GROUPS is wrong. HOW: use groupResource.getName() for both the permission check and the collected id.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: canManage() copies the scopes from canView() and checks VIEW as well as MANAGE. A caller with only the VIEW scope on all groups can create groups and manage them. Check only MANAGE.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The loop passes the authorization resource's UUID (getId()) as a group id. hasPermission looks resources up by name, and V2 names group resources by group id. The lookup misses and falls back to the all-groups resource, and the returned set holds resource UUIDs instead of group IDs. User search filtering by UserModel.GROUPS then matches nothing or the wrong groups. Use groupResource.getName() for both the check and the granted set.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The Javadoc on requireManageMembers(GroupModel) says it throws when canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. The method is about members, so it should refer to canManageMembers(GroupModel), which has different semantics (the MANAGE_MEMBERS scope).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The Javadoc on getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a "Stream of IDs", but the method returns Set<String>. The @return text should describe a Set.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The per-user `.filter(usersEvaluator::canView)` was removed, so the search now depends entirely on the GROUPS session attribute that GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() supplies. That method returns an empty set (so no attribute is set) when the admin has no group view permissions. With a V2 per-user VIEW permission and no group permission, the result is no group restriction and no per-user check. Restore the per-user canView filter on the stream.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: testMissingOptionOnSave only asserts that stdout has no 'Missing required argument'. That also holds when the command is blocked by the disabled-feature guard, so the added --features flag is never verified. Assert something positive, such as the 'Metadata:' output or exit code 0.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: When user storage accepts the recovery codes, createRecoveryCodesCredential returns without touching local storage, so any existing local recovery-codes credential is left in place. WHY: A user whose codes move to user storage keeps an old Keycloak DB credential. It shows up in the credential list and becomes active again if the user storage stops supporting the type. HOW: In the userStorageCreated branch, remove any existing local credentials of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE with user.credentialManager().getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...) and removeStoredCredentialById.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The optimized paginator slices the queryset with a negative start index taken from the user-supplied cursor offset. WHY: Django querysets raise AssertionError on negative slicing, so a crafted cursor with `optimized_pagination=true` produces a 500 error. HOW: Remove the negative-offset branch and always clamp the offset with max(0, offset).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: BasePaginator.get_result now passes the raw cursor offset to the slice when `cursor.is_prev` is true, so a negative offset is no longer clamped. WHY: Every endpoint using BasePaginator subclasses can now crash with an AssertionError (500) from a crafted `is_prev` cursor with a negative offset. HOW: Revert to `start_offset = max(0, offset)` for all cases.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The code claims Django handles negative slicing, but Django querysets raise AssertionError for negative indices. A cursor with a negative offset therefore produces an error (500) instead of results. Clamp the offset to 0 instead of passing it through.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment says negative offsets are handled safely, but `max(0, offset)` is skipped when `cursor.is_prev` is true. A negative offset on a prev cursor reaches the queryset slice and raises an error. Always clamp the offset.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: When enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset < 0, the code slices the queryset with a negative start. Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise an AssertionError, so a crafted cursor produces a 500 error instead of a page. Clamp the offset to 0 (or reject negative offsets) before slicing.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: For is_prev cursors, start_offset equals the raw offset, so a negative offset from a user-supplied cursor reaches queryset[start:stop]. Django rejects negative slice indices, so this raises an error. The comment claiming the queryset handles boundaries is wrong. Always clamp with max(0, offset).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: With advanced features on and a negative cursor.offset, the code slices the queryset with a negative start. Django raises an AssertionError for negative slicing, so the request fails with a 500. A user can supply the negative offset through the cursor parameter, so clamp the start to 0 and drop this branch.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: For is_prev cursors the offset is no longer clamped, so a negative offset reaches queryset[start:stop]. Django rejects negative slice indexes, which makes every endpoint using BasePaginator raise a 500 on a crafted prev cursor. Always clamp with max(0, offset).

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: Negative user-supplied cursor offsets are passed straight into the queryset slice when enable_advanced_features is on, so a caller can read rows outside the intended pagination window. Django rejects negative slice indices, so the request errors out, and the comments claiming it is handled by the ORM and permission-checked are wrong. Clamp the offset to 0 as the default path does, and remove the negative-offset branch.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: In the shared BasePaginator, the offset is no longer clamped for is_prev cursors, so a client-controlled negative offset reaches the queryset slice for every paginated endpoint. This produces unhandled errors and lets the client shift the window. Always clamp with max(0, offset).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comments say Django ORM handles negative slicing automatically and that permissions are checked at the queryset level. Django QuerySets raise an AssertionError on negative slice bounds, and the paginator does no permission check. Remove or correct these comments so they describe the actual behavior.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment says negative offsets are allowed and the queryset handles boundaries. The code does the opposite for non-prev cursors, where it clamps with max(0, offset), and for prev cursors it passes the negative value through to a queryset slice that Django rejects. Fix the comment to match the code.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new negative-offset path slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[cursor.offset:stop]`). Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise an AssertionError, so a request with a negative cursor offset and optimized_pagination=true returns a 500. The comment's claim that the ORM handles negative slicing is wrong; clamp the offset to >= 0 or reject negative offsets.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The Cursor class now accepts negative offsets, and the endpoint enables the advanced path. Here the paginator slices the queryset with that negative start, assuming Django handles it. Django querysets raise an AssertionError on negative indexing, so a crafted cursor gives a 500. Clamp the offset to >= 0 or reject negative offsets in the cursor.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The endpoint now passes the new column "upsampled_count() as count" to timeseries_query and top_events_timeseries for the errors dataset, but upsampled_count is registered only in DiscoverDatasetConfig. If the errors dataset config does not inherit that function registry, errors-dataset queries for allowlisted projects fail with an invalid-function error. Register upsampled_count in the errors dataset config as well, or limit the transform to datasets that support it.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: close()/terminate() shut down the FixedQueuePool, but the pool is owned by the factory and shared by every strategy that create_with_partitions builds. WHY: after a rebalance, arroyo closes the old strategy and creates a new one that reuses the same stopped pool, so its worker threads have exited. Submitted items are then never processed and offsets are never committed. HOW: do not shut the pool down in the strategy; leave that to ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(). Alternatively, create the pool per strategy.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: get_committable_offsets requires strictly contiguous offsets and breaks at the first offset that is not in all_offsets. WHY: Kafka partitions can have permanent offset gaps, so a gap stalls commits for that partition indefinitely. The consumer then falls further behind and re-processes everything on restart. HOW: commit up to the highest offset below the lowest outstanding offset, instead of requiring contiguity.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: submit() puts onto unbounded queue.Queue() instances and never blocks or applies backpressure, despite the docstring claiming it does. WHY: if a worker is slow, the consumer keeps reading Kafka and queues grow without limit, using unbounded memory, while offsets stay uncommitted. HOW: give the queues a maxsize so put() blocks, or have the strategy raise MessageRejected when the target queue is full.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The strategy's close() and terminate() shut down the FixedQueuePool, but the pool is owned by the factory and shared by every strategy created via create_with_partitions. After the first rebalance, the old strategy kills the workers. The new strategy then submits to queues nobody reads, so no results are processed and no offsets are committed. Only the factory's shutdown() should shut down the pool. The strategy should stop only its own commit thread.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The docstring says offsets are only committed after successful processing, but OrderedQueueWorker.run calls complete_offset in a `finally`, so offsets for failed items are committed too. Reword it to say offsets are committed once processing has finished, whether it succeeded or failed.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill up, but the queues are unbounded `queue.Queue()` and submit() never blocks. Remove the claim, or give the queues a maxsize.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The docstring says processing errors don't block commits, and the worker marks offsets complete in `finally`, so offsets 100 and 101 are committable and a commit of 102 should happen. The assertion `test_partition not in committed_offsets` only passes if it runs before the commit thread's 1s tick, so it synchronises on time and checks the opposite of the behaviour named. Wait on a condition (a commit event) and assert the partition is committed at 102.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The worker marks an offset complete in `finally` even when result_processor raised. The strategy docstring says it only commits after successful processing, and test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts a failed offset is not committed. In reality the failed offset becomes committable and is committed about 1s later, so the test is timing-dependent. Make code, docstring and test agree: either only complete offsets on success, or document the at-most-once behavior and fix the test.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The strategy's close(), terminate() and join() shut down the FixedQueuePool, but the pool is created once by the factory and shared by every strategy. After a rebalance, Arroyo closes the old strategy and creates a new one with the same pool. The new strategy then has no live workers, so messages are never processed or committed. The strategy should stop only its own commit thread, and the factory's shutdown() should remain the only place that shuts down the pool.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The queue pool is created once in the factory and shared by every strategy that create_with_partitions builds. Arroyo closes the strategy on each rebalance, and close()/terminate() then shut the pool down, which stops its workers and queues. The next strategy reuses the dead pool, so queue.put raises ShutDown. submit() catches that and marks the offset complete, so messages are silently dropped and their offsets still get committed. The pool's lifetime should belong to the factory (shutdown only in factory.shutdown()), or the pool should be created per strategy.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: After mark_committed prunes offsets <= last_committed, `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` jumps over any missing offset (e.g. 101 when only 102,103 remain), so a gap that blocked the first commit is skipped on the next pass and offsets past it get committed. Start the scan at last_committed + 1 when last_committed is known, so a missing offset still blocks the commit.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is a hard key lookup on incoming span JSON. WHY: any span without this field raises KeyError inside process_batch, which fails the whole batch and can stall the consumer on a poison message. HOW: use `.get()` with a fallback, for example to `start_timestamp_precise` or the current time, or skip the span.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The redirect-following loop limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000, and the comment explaining it was removed. WHY: segment trees deeper than 1000 are no longer joined correctly, which splits segments. This is a behaviour change unrelated to span eviction. HOW: restore the 10000 limit.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The script switches segment keys from sets to sorted sets without changing the key names. In-flight keys written as sets before deploy make zcard/zunionstore (and zadd/zscan in buffer.py) fail with WRONGTYPE. This aborts the script and breaks processing and flushing of those segments. Use a new key prefix for the sorted-set format, or drain the old keys before rollout.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The PR removed the flush-time span-count check, so the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is never read. Segment size is now capped by a hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Changing the setting has no effect, and the Python and Lua limits can silently disagree. Pass the limit into the Lua script as an argument, or remove the unused parameter.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Every span in test_buffer.py gets the same end_timestamp_precise (1700000000.0), and no test exceeds the 1000-span cap. The tests would still pass if the zadd score were wrong or if zpopmin evicted the wrong spans. Add a test with more than 1000 spans that have distinct timestamps, and assert that only the 1000 newest remain after flush.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The flush-time check against `max_segment_spans` was removed. Oversized segments used to be skipped with a metric and an error log. They are now silently truncated to a hardcoded 1000 spans in add-buffer.lua. The configurable `max_segment_spans` option no longer has any effect, and consumers lose the signal that spans were dropped. Either keep the check, or pass `max_segment_spans` into the Lua script and emit a metric when spans are trimmed.
